body.objective: Students will be able to use the four-step critique.
body.iCan: I can use the four-step critique.
successCriteria: I can describe an artwork objectively
I can analyze how the elements and principles are used
I can interpret meaning and judge an artwork with evidence
body.hook: Two people can look at the same painting and see completely different things. A critique isn't about saying "I like it" or "I don't." It's a step-by-step way of looking that lets you back up what you think with what you see.

vocabulary.definition: A structured discussion that describes, analyzes, interprets and judges an artwork.
To list what you see without giving opinions.
To explain how the elements and principles of design are organized.
An explanation of what an artwork means, backed by evidence.
Using an object, colour or image to stand for an idea.
The time, place and culture in which an artwork was made.
Ideas about beauty and what makes art meaningful or successful.

study.title: Four Steps to Seeing
study.question: How can we look closely at art from any culture and respond with evidence?
study.passage:
Choose three artworks from different cultures and times, for example: a Haida bentwood box or button blanket, Katsushika Hokusai's "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" (Japan, about 1831), and a work by a contemporary Canadian artist.
Step 1, Describe (What do I see?): List subject, colours, lines, shapes, textures, medium and size. No opinions yet.
Step 2, Analyze (How is it organized?): Which elements and principles stand out? Where is the focal point? How does the eye move? How is balance or rhythm created?
Step 3, Interpret (What does it mean?): What mood or message does it suggest? What symbols appear? What does the context (culture, time, purpose) add? Use "I think ... because I see ..."
Step 4, Judge (Is it successful?): Decide whether the work succeeds and by which criteria: skill, expression, originality or function.
Respect: When looking at Indigenous and other cultural works, learn what the work means to the culture that made it, use the correct names, and remember that some objects are ceremonial, not decorative.
study.source: Original critique activity written for this lesson using the Feldman four-step model.
discussion: Why is it important to describe before you judge?
How did context change your interpretation?
Did classmates interpret the same work differently? Were both supported?
What criteria should we use to judge art from another culture?
study.product: Write a four-paragraph critique (one paragraph per step) of an artwork from a culture other than your own, including at least one fact about its context.

examples.title: Describe
examples.answer: A huge curling wave with claw-like foam, small boats and Mount Fuji in the distance, in blues and white
examples.explore: What details might you miss at first glance?

examples.title: Analyze
examples.problem: Where is the focal point of "The Great Wave"?
examples.answer: The curling crest of the wave, which frames Mount Fuji
examples.explore: How does the curve move your eye?

examples.title: Interpret
examples.problem: What might the work say about people and nature?
examples.answer: Nature is powerful and people are small or vulnerable
examples.explore: What other interpretations could the image support?

examples.title: Judge
examples.problem: Is the work successful? Use a criterion.
examples.answer: Yes, on expression: the dramatic composition makes the viewer feel the wave's power
examples.explore: Would your judgment change with a different criterion?

practice.q: Name the four steps of a critique.
What do you do in the describe step?
practice.a: List what you see without opinions.
Using an image or colour to stand for an idea.
The time, place and culture an artwork comes from.
The area that draws the eye first.
So opinions are based on evidence.

practice.q: What questions guide the analyze step?
practice.a: How are the elements and principles organized? Where does the eye go?

practice.q: Give two criteria for judging art.
practice.a: Technical skill, expression, originality or function.
It reveals meanings the image alone might not show.

practice.q: Why use the correct names for cultural works?
Two students interpret a work differently. Can both be right?
practice.a: Yes, if both are supported by evidence from the work and its context.

practice.q: Why might judging a ceremonial object only on beauty be unfair?
practice.a: Its purpose and meaning in its culture matter more than decoration.

practice.q: How does an artist's culture shape an artwork?
practice.a: Through materials, symbols, beliefs, stories and purpose.

practice.q: Revise "This painting is ugly" into a judgment with criteria.
practice.a: For example: The composition feels unbalanced because all the weight is on the left.

misconceptions: Thinking there is one correct interpretation
Judging art from other cultures only by one's own standards
exitTicket: Name the four steps of a critique in order.
Write one interpretation using "I think ... because I see ..."

test.title: Practice test: Use the four-step critique

items.q: The first step of a critique is
items.answer: C) describe

items.q: In the describe step, you should
options: B) list what you see without opinions
items.answer: B) list what you see without opinions

items.q: Context means
options: A) the frame around a work
B) the time, place and culture of a work
C) the price of a work
items.answer: B) the time, place and culture of a work

items.q: Symbolism is
options: A) using an image to stand for an idea
items.answer: A) using an image to stand for an idea

items.q: Which question belongs to the analyze step?
options: B) Is it the best artwork ever?
C) How are the elements and principles organized?
D) What does it mean to me?
items.answer: C) How are the elements and principles organized?

items.q: A good interpretation is
options: A) supported by evidence in the work
items.answer: A) supported by evidence in the work

items.q: Which is a criterion for judging art?
items.answer: D) expression

items.q: Why research context before interpreting?
options: B) It is required by law
D) It can reveal meaning the image alone does not
items.answer: D) It can reveal meaning the image alone does not

items.q: A focal point is
options: A) the edge of the work
B) where the eye goes first
items.answer: B) where the eye goes first

items.q: Two different interpretations of one work are both valid when
options: D) both are supported by evidence
items.answer: D) both are supported by evidence

items.q: When responding to a ceremonial Indigenous object, it is most important to
options: B) learn its meaning to the culture that made it
C) compare its price to other works
items.answer: B) learn its meaning to the culture that made it

items.q: Which statement is a judgment with criteria?
options: C) The strong contrast makes the message powerful.
items.answer: C) The strong contrast makes the message powerful.

items.q: List the four critique steps.
items.answer: Describe, analyze, interpret, judge.

items.q: What is an interpretation?
items.answer: An explanation of an artwork's meaning backed by evidence.

items.q: Describe the difference between describing and analyzing.
items.answer: Describing lists what you see; analyzing explains how it is organized.

items.q: Why does context matter in a critique?
items.answer: It helps explain purpose, symbols and meaning.

items.q: Give one symbol you might see in an artwork and its meaning.
items.answer: Answers vary, for example a dove for peace.

items.q: Name two criteria for judging art.
items.answer: For example skill and expression.

items.q: Explain how to respond respectfully to art from another culture.
items.answer: Learn its meaning and purpose from that culture, use correct names and avoid judging by one's own standards only.

items.q: Write a short judgment of an artwork you know, with a criterion and evidence.
items.answer: Answers vary; must name a criterion and evidence.
